description: Input validation, least privilege, crypto basics

screens.body:
Rule zero of secure coding: never trust input. Not from forms, not from URLs, not from APIs, not even from your own frontend — attackers bypass frontends in seconds with dev tools.

Validate everything on the SERVER: right type, right range, right format. The frontend validates for user experience; the server validates for security.

options: On the server — frontends are bypassable
Only in the frontend
Only for logged-out users
check.question: Where must validation happen?

screens.heading: Never trust input
screens.keyPoint: Frontend validates for UX; server validates for safety.

screens.body:
Two validation philosophies: denylist ('block these bad things') and allowlist ('only these good things pass'). Denylists always lose — attackers invent a new bad thing you didn't list.

Allowlist everything you can: this field accepts letters and spaces only; this upload accepts .png under 2MB. Define good, reject the rest.

options: Denylist — block known bad things
Allowlist — define good, reject the rest
No validation needed
check.question: The winning validation philosophy:

screens.heading: Allowlist, don't denylist

screens.body:
Least privilege: every user, service, and line of code gets the MINIMUM power it needs — nothing more. Your app's database user should read/write app tables, not drop the whole database.

When (not if) something gets compromised, least privilege contains the blast radius. A read-only key leaking is a bad day; an admin key leaking is a catastrophe.

options: Give everything admin rights for simplicity
Minimum power needed — contain the blast radius
Trust all internal code completely
check.question: Least privilege means…

screens.heading: Minimum power, always
screens.keyPoint: Leaks happen. Limit what a leak can do.

screens.body:
Secrets — API keys, database passwords, tokens — live in environment variables or a secret manager. NEVER in code, never in git history, never in a Slack message.

One leaked key in a public repo gets harvested by bots within minutes. If a secret touches git, rotate it (generate a new one) — deleting the commit isn't enough, history remembers.

options: In the code — it's private
In a group chat for the team
Env vars or a secret manager; rotate if ever exposed
check.question: Where do secrets live?

screens.heading: Secrets stay secret
screens.keyPoint: Env vars, not git. Leaked = rotated.

screens.body:
Crypto basics in two distinctions: hashing is one-way (passwords — you never un-hash), encryption is two-way (data you need to read back later, like stored credit-card tokens).

And the golden rule: never invent your own crypto. Use vetted libraries (bcrypt for passwords, TLS for transit). Cryptography is where cleverness goes to die.

options: Hashing is one-way, encryption is reversible — and never roll your own
They're the same thing
Write your own for extra security
check.question: Crypto basics:

screens.heading: Hash vs encrypt, and don't DIY
screens.keyPoint: Use vetted libraries. Never invent crypto.

screens.body:
Errors are information. Show users 'Something went wrong, try again' — log the full stack trace privately. A detailed error page can hand attackers your database schema, file paths, and library versions.

Same for failed logins: 'Invalid email or password' — never 'that email doesn't exist,' which lets attackers harvest registered accounts.

options: Show full stack traces to users
Generic message to users, details to private logs
Hide all errors silently
check.question: Secure error handling:

screens.heading: Errors talk — keep them quiet
screens.keyPoint: Users get generics; logs get details.

screens.body:
Your dependencies are code you didn't write running with your privileges. Outdated packages are one of the most common breach vectors — the fix is routine: lockfiles, `npm audit`, and updating on a schedule.

Before adding a package, glance at its health: maintained? popular enough? tiny and focused? Every dependency is trust you're extending.

options: Add packages freely, never update
Audit, lock, and update dependencies routinely
Only use code you wrote
check.question: Dependency hygiene:

screens.heading: Your dependencies are attack surface
screens.keyPoint: Audit, lock, update — on a schedule.
